\begin{abstract}
The consistent-but-dangerous taxonomy flags a medical vision-language model (VLM) answer as \dang{} when it is
stable under paraphrase and unchanged when the image is removed. We test whether image removal measures image
reliance well enough to compare models. Three medical VLMs and their general-purpose bases (MedGemma-4B and
MedGemma-1.5-4B \vs Gemma-3-4B; MedVLThinker-3B \vs Qwen2.5-VL-3B) answer 3,365 questions over 907 CT, MRI,
X-ray and pathology images with the image removed and under three probes that keep an image in the input: a
wrong image, a black image, and an image on which the same question has the opposite answer. Endpoints were
pre-registered, and every later probe and model pair was registered before it was run. Image removal finds
MedGemma more ``consistent but blind'' than Gemma-3 (\dang{} share +13.7 points\ci{10.0}{17.5}). No in-format
probe agrees: of nine pair-by-dataset comparisons, image removal separates the models in five, and an
in-format probe confirms none of them. Its differences follow refusal instead (forced to answer yes or no
without an image, Gemma-3 would rather ask for it on 29\% of questions, and its forced answers there are
unrelated to its answers with the image) and agreement between a model's priors and the image; MedGemma's excess
\dang{} answers are all correct. The in-format probes need care too: the MedGemmas follow opposite-answer images
far more than Gemma-3 on SLAKE, which they were trained on (+48 and +37 points), but not on PathVQA, which no
medical model was trained on (+0.8 and $-5.6$; pre-registered). The \dang{} share also rests on a 36--42\% chance
floor on yes/no questions, and image reliance does not flag wrong answers (AUROC 0.51). Comparing models on
image reliance requires in-format probes on data outside their training sets.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
A model that answers a question about an image without using the image is not doing visual question
answering, however accurate it is. In general-domain VQA this concern produced balanced benchmarks and
prior-robust splits~\cite{goyal2017vqav2,agrawal2018dont}. Medical VQA is still mostly evaluated by accuracy,
where it matters more: a correct answer reached from language priors will be wrong on exactly the patients
whose images are unusual.

Accuracy cannot separate \emph{seeing} from \emph{guessing well}, and consistency under rephrasing cannot either:
a model that ignores the image is often \emph{more} consistent, because nothing visual perturbs
it~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed}. Sadanandan and Behzadan~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} therefore crossed the two
per sample. \emph{Consistent} means the answer is stable under paraphrase; \emph{image-reliant} means it changes
when the image is removed. This gives four quadrants: \textsc{Ideal} (consistent, reliant), \textsc{Fragile},
\dang{} (consistent but unchanged without the image) and \textsc{Worst}. On chest X-rays they found that
fine-tuning for consistency moves most answers into \dang{}.

A taxonomy like this invites comparisons between models, and a comparison is only as good as the probe behind
it. Removing the image changes the input format: a model asked about an image that is not there may refuse,
answer from priors, or guess, and none of these is the same as ignoring an image that is present. We therefore
compare image removal with probes that keep an image in the input, on the same questions and for three medical
VLMs, each against the general model it shares an architecture with: MedGemma-4B~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma}
and MedGemma-1.5-4B against Gemma-3-4B~\cite{gemma2025gemma3}, and MedVLThinker-3B against its base
Qwen2.5-VL-3B, on CT, MRI, X-ray and pathology questions from three public benchmarks.

\Cref{fig:bydataset} summarizes the answer. Image removal reports differences between medical and general models
that no in-format probe confirms, in every dataset and pair where it reports one. The in-format probes in turn
find the MedGemmas far more image-reliant only on SLAKE, a dataset both were trained on; on PathVQA, which no
medical model was trained on, a pre-registered test finds no advantage.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item A side-by-side comparison of four reliance probes on the same questions for three medical/general model
pairs and three datasets, showing that image removal's between-model differences are confirmed by no in-format
probe. Each probe has precedent~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent,zafar2026see,lotfinia2026cxr}; to our knowledge
their verdicts about the same models have not been compared.
\item Direct evidence for what image removal picks up instead: refusal under a forced yes/no format, and agreement
between a model's prior and the image.
\item A pre-registered out-of-distribution test showing that two medical models' large in-format advantage on
their training distribution does not transfer, so in-format probes also need held-out data.
\item Two corrections to the \dang{} share: its chance floor on yes/no questions (with Cohen's $\kappa$), and a
paired split into correct and wrong \dang{} answers.
\item A pre-registered, open pipeline across three datasets, four modalities and five models, with a paraphrase
set screened pair by pair for equivalence and a finding that bf16 batching perturbs log-probabilities by up to
1~nat.
\end{itemize}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}
\paragraph{Language priors in VQA.} Balanced pairs~\cite{goyal2017vqav2} and changing-prior
splits~\cite{agrawal2018dont} showed that general VQA models exploit answer priors; text-only baselines are the
medical analogue.

\paragraph{Does a medical VLM use the image?} PSF-Med~\cite{sadanandan2026psfmed} measured paraphrase flip rates
across medical VLMs on chest X-rays and noted that low flip rates often come with high text-only agreement. The
quadrant taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent} defines reliance by image removal and corroborates it with a
KL-divergence score, a black image and random image swaps; on their models these checks agreed with image removal.
Zafar~\etal~\cite{zafar2026see} build blank, pixel-shuffled, absent and CLIP-retrieved hard-negative images to
define reliance metrics and train a model against them. Lotfinia~\etal~\cite{lotfinia2026cxr} swap and occlude
chest radiographs and find that model class (medical or general) does not predict image use. Pathology VLMs reach
high accuracy without the image~\cite{zhang2026pathology}, and medical MLLMs often attend to irrelevant
regions~\cite{liu2026medmllmfail}. Grounding inputs can even hurt closed-ended accuracy~\cite{chen2026grounding};
HEAL-MedVQA~\cite{nguyen2025heal} and MedHEval~\cite{chang2025medheval} benchmark localization and hallucination.
These works use one probe or treat several as interchangeable; we compare their verdicts on the same models, and
inside and outside the models' training data.

\paragraph{Answering without the evidence.} MedVIGIL~\cite{jiang2026medvigil} tests whether models refuse when
visual evidence is broken, and Vohra~\cite{vohra2026hearsay} finds that frontier VLMs confabulate diagnoses for
images that were never attached. Four of our five small open models decline almost always when allowed to; we
show what forcing an answer does to a reliance probe.

\paragraph{Selective prediction.} Ranking answers by a score and abstaining on the lowest is evaluated by AUROC
and risk--coverage~\cite{geifman2017selective}; we use it to ask whether reliance flags errors.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
\subsection{Data}
\textbf{SLAKE}~\cite{liu2021slake} (English; CT, MRI, X-ray; 2,114 questions from test and validation, the
only dataset with modality labels; validation is added so each modality has 53--82 images).
\textbf{VQA-RAD}~\cite{lau2018vqarad} (radiology, clinician-written; all 451 test questions, from the
original release). \textbf{PathVQA}~\cite{he2020pathvqa} (pathology, generated from textbook captions; 600
yes/no and 200 open test questions sampled with a fixed seed). A question is yes/no if its gold answer is
\emph{yes} or \emph{no}. The \textbf{primary analysis set} is the 1,206 yes/no \emph{test} questions on 670
images. Probe R4 uses a separate set: all 1,192 PathVQA test and validation yes/no questions that are also asked
about another image with the opposite answer (682 images). Sampling, partner images and image hashes are fixed in
committed manifests (SHA-1 seeded), so every run sees identical inputs.

\subsection{Models}
\textbf{MedGemma-4B} (\texttt{google/medgemma-4b-it}) is an open medical VLM whose SigLIP-style
encoder~\cite{zhai2023siglip} and language model were further trained on medical data; its technical
report~\cite{sellergren2025medgemma} lists SLAKE (450 items, the size of SLAKE's train split) and VQA-RAD
(reinforcement-learning stage) among its training data and states that PathVQA was removed. \textbf{Gemma-3-4B}
(\texttt{google/gemma-3-4b-it}) shares its architecture and size. \textbf{MedGemma-1.5-4B}
(\texttt{google/medgemma-1.5-4b-it}, the 2026 release; its card lists SLAKE) is compared with the same Gemma-3-4B,
and \textbf{MedVLThinker-3B} (\texttt{UCSC-VLAA/MedVLThinker-3B-RL\_PMC}, Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct trained with
reinforcement learning on PMC-VQA) with its base \textbf{Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct}. A medical model and its base
differ in their whole post-training, not only in medical data, so we compare \emph{checkpoints}. All five run
unquantized in bf16 on one 16\,GB GPU (quantization would perturb the probabilities we audit) and receive
identical prompts: a fixed system line, the question, and ``Answer with only `yes' or `no'.'' or ``Answer with a
single word or short phrase.'' Each model added after the primary pair passed a registered format check first
(mean yes/no first-token mass with the image $\ge0.9$ in every dataset of a 330-question pilot; 0.93--0.999).

\subsection{Probes}
\label{sec:probes}
Every question is posed with its image (\textbf{orig}) and with screened paraphrases (\textbf{para$_k$},
original image; \cref{sec:para}). Reliance is probed by changing only the image or the instruction:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
\item \textbf{Image removed} (\emph{noimg}): image tokens omitted, text identical; the reference probe of the
taxonomy~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}.
\item \textbf{Wrong image} (\emph{shuf}): another image from the same dataset and modality, chosen by a hash of
the question ID.
\item \textbf{R1, black image}: a black image in the image slot, in format but without content.
\item \textbf{R2, ``unknown'' allowed}: image removed, and the instruction adds ``If this cannot be determined
without seeing the image, answer `unknown'.''
\item \textbf{R3, opposite-answer image}: another image of the same dataset and modality on which the
\emph{same} question has the opposite gold answer; a model that uses the image must change its answer. Partners
exist for 367 SLAKE yes/no questions (130 images), whose templated questions recur across images.
\item \textbf{R4}: R3 on the 1,192 PathVQA questions above, outside every medical model's listed training data.
\end{itemize}
The first two belong to the pre-registered main run; R1--R4 and the two added model pairs were each registered
after the results that motivated them and before they were run.

\subsection{Measures}
\textbf{Yes/no answers} come from one forward pass:
$P(\text{yes})=\sigma(\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in Y}\,\ell_t-\mathrm{LSE}_{t\in N}\,\ell_t)$ over the single-token
variants of \emph{yes} and \emph{no}; the first-token mass $m=P(Y)+P(N)$ is logged as a format check.
\textbf{Open answers} use greedy decoding and token-F1$\,\ge0.5$ after normalization, with an opposite-term
guard (left/right, upper/lower, \etc never match). \textbf{Consistent}: the answer on the first two valid
paraphrases equals the \emph{orig} answer. \textbf{Reliant} under a probe: the probe answer differs from
\emph{orig}; across probes we compare this \emph{answer-change rate}. The \textbf{quadrant} follows from
(consistent, reliant). \textbf{Refusal}: $m<0.5$, \ie most first-token mass is on neither \emph{yes} nor
\emph{no}; free generation confirms these are requests for the image (\cref{fig:teaser}a). \textbf{Pair accuracy}
(R3, R4): right on both images, 0 by construction for a model that ignores the image. \textbf{Image PMI} of an
answer $\hat y$ is $\log p(\hat y\mid I,q)-\log p(\hat y\mid\varnothing,q)$. \textbf{Chance correction}: Cohen's
$\kappa$~\cite{cohen1960kappa} between \emph{orig} and probe answers; the \emph{chance floor} of the \dang{} share
is $P(\text{consistent})\cdot p_e$, where $p_e$ is the agreement expected from the two answer distributions alone.

\subsection{Paraphrase construction and screening}
\label{sec:para}
Paraphrase consistency is meaningful only if a paraphrase cannot change the correct answer. Candidates come
from Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct~\cite{qwen2024qwen25} (greedy; five styles) and from two deterministic templates that copy
every content word (``Is there X?''$\to$``Is X present?''). A rule validator rejects changes to laterality,
negation and absence words, quantities, antonyms, imaging planes, question form, answer leakage, near-copies and
length. Two audit rounds accepted 81\% and 83\%, below the pre-specified 85\%, so we tightened the rules,
excluded a ``plain language'' style, and \textbf{judged every unique rule-valid (question, paraphrase) pair},
4,890 in total, against a written rubric (\cref{app:rubric}). The judge was an LLM (Claude); see
\cref{sec:limits}. 1,208 pairs were rejected, each with a recorded reason (\eg \emph{mass$\to$lesion}, \emph{is
enlarged$\to$can be enlarged}), and unjudged pairs are rejected by construction. 84\% of the primary-set
questions retain at least two valid paraphrases; quadrant analyses use those (1,012 questions, 600 images).

\subsection{Statistics and pre-registration}
Hypotheses, endpoints, tests and exclusions were frozen before the main run~\cite{nosek2018prereg}; every later
change is listed in \cref{app:dev}, and post-hoc analyses are labeled as such. Several questions share an image,
so all intervals are percentile 95\% CIs from a cluster bootstrap over images~\cite{field2007bootstrap}
($B=2000$) with two-sided bootstrap $p$-values. Holm families~\cite{holm1979} (\cref{tab:tests}): \textbf{P1a--c}
(blind accuracy minus the majority-answer prior) and \textbf{P2} (AUROC of image PMI minus AUROC of confidence);
\textbf{H6--H8} (probes R1--R3, MedGemma $-$ Gemma-3); \textbf{H9--H11} (added pairs, medical $-$ general:
follows R3 more, changes less without the image, refuses less); and \textbf{H12a--c} (R4, with a decision rule
fixed in advance). \textbf{P3}, the paired difference in \dang{} share, is a family of its own. A finding is called
robust only if its sign holds across a grid of F1 thresholds (0.3/0.5/0.8), paraphrase counts (1/2/3) and
``strong'' flips.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
All runs completed (18,896 calls per model in the main run, 3,535 for R1--R3 and 2,384 for R4, five models). Our
pipeline reproduces MedGemma's published SLAKE score (token-F1 70.2\ci{67.5}{72.7} \vs 72.3 on the model card;
Gemma-3: 45.1 \vs 40.2), and the yes/no format mass with the image is $\ge0.997$ in every dataset. MedGemma is
the more accurate model with the image (\cref{tab:acc}) by 18 points on SLAKE and 25 on VQA-RAD yes/no, both
in its training data, and by 2 on PathVQA, which is not.

\subsection{The reference probe: MedGemma looks more consistent but blind}
\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_quadrants.png}
\caption{Quadrant composition of yes/no answers (test), MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3-4B. Left: reliance probed by
removing the image (the reference definition). Right: by a wrong image of the same modality. Shares are raw; on
yes/no questions they include chance agreement (\cref{sec:chance}) and correct answers (\cref{sec:what}).}
\label{fig:quad}
\end{figure*}

Under image removal MedGemma's \dang{} share is 50.6/46.8/56.5\% (PathVQA/SLAKE/VQA-RAD) against
43.2/28.1/31.0\% for Gemma-3 (\cref{fig:quad}, left). The paired difference, \textbf{P3 $=+13.7$
points}\ci{10.0}{17.5} ($p<0.001$; 1,012 questions, 600 images), is positive in every dataset (PathVQA
+7.5\ci{2.6}{12.3}, SLAKE +18.6\ci{12.2}{24.9}, VQA-RAD +25.6\ci{14.7}{36.5}) and in every cell of the
sensitivity grid. MedGemma is also the more consistent model (paraphrase flip rate 6.8\% \vs 13.6\% on SLAKE).
MedGemma-1.5 shows the same pattern (+9.8\ci{5.8}{13.9}). Read at face value, the medical checkpoints are more
often stable, confident and blind.

\subsection{No in-format probe agrees with image removal}
\label{sec:disagree}
\Cref{fig:bydataset} puts every probe on one scale, the share of answers that change, and splits it by pair and
dataset. Image removal separates the medical model from its base in five of the nine cells: lower change rates
for both MedGemmas on VQA-RAD ($-19.1$\ci{$-27.6$}{$-10.4$} and $-18.7$\ci{$-27.3$}{$-9.4$}) and for MedGemma-4B
on SLAKE ($-9.9$\ci{$-14.9$}{$-4.4$}), higher ones for MedVLThinker on PathVQA and VQA-RAD (+4.5\ci{1.7}{7.2},
+11.2\ci{5.3}{17.4}). In four of these cells no in-format probe finds any difference; in the fifth, MedGemma-4B on
SLAKE, every in-format probe finds the opposite (wrong image +11.8, black image +33.0, opposite-answer image +48.0
points). Pooled over datasets the primary pair shows the same split: image removal $-6.1$\ci{$-9.5$}{$-2.7$},
wrong image +5.1\ci{1.7}{8.5}, black image +20.3\ci{15.9}{24.6}. The two main-run probes also disagree per
question ($\kappa$ between their reliance labels $-0.11$ to 0.23), and the modality ordering of the \dang{}
share reverses between them (X-ray lowest under image removal, highest under a wrong image), partly because a
random partner often has the same correct answer (all 23 chest X-ray partners that carry the same question).

\paragraph{The in-format probes on SLAKE.} The registered probes R1 and R3 were run on the primary pair after the
main results. H6 predicted that MedGemma's answers would survive a black image more often; it failed in the
opposite direction ($\kappa(\text{image},\text{black})=0.11$ \vs 0.33): on a black image MedGemma's yes-rate drops
from 58\% to 28\% (it reads an empty image as absent findings), while Gemma-3's rises from 64\% to 84\%. H8 held:
on SLAKE's opposite-answer swaps MedGemma follows the image 72.8\% of the time and Gemma-3 24.8\%, and
MedGemma is right on both images in 71.7\% of swaps against 23.4\%. MedGemma-1.5 replicates this on SLAKE (H9,
+36.5\ci{30.6}{42.1}); MedVLThinker does not differ from its base under any in-format probe on any dataset except
a small black-image difference on SLAKE ($-3.4$\ci{$-6.5$}{$-0.3$}). \Cref{sec:r4} tests whether the MedGemma
advantage holds outside SLAKE.

\subsection{What image removal picks up}
\label{sec:what}
\paragraph{Refusal.} The pre-registered format check ($m\ge0.9$) failed in exactly one condition, image removed.
Free generation explains it: ``\emph{Please provide the picture. I need to see the image to determine if there
is a spinal cord present}'' (Gemma-3). Gemma-3 would rather refuse on 354 of the 1,206 questions, MedGemma-4B on
219 and MedGemma-1.5 on 8 (\cref{fig:abst}); MedVLThinker and Qwen2.5-VL never refuse. On refused questions the
forced answer is mostly \emph{no} and unrelated to the model's answer with the image ($\kappa=-0.01$ for Gemma-3,
0.04 for MedGemma), so 53--55\% of them count as ``image-reliant''. Image removal's largest differences sit where
refusal differs most: on VQA-RAD Gemma-3 refuses on half the questions, 23 points more than MedGemma-4B and 48 more
than MedGemma-1.5. Allowed to say ``unknown'' (R2), MedGemma-4B declines on 93.0\% and Gemma-3 on 99.7\% (H7,
$-6.7$), so most of the forced-format difference of 11.2 points disappears. For MedGemma-1.5, which refuses on
almost nothing, the \dang{} gap shrinks to +3.0\ci{$-3.6$}{9.5} on the 467 questions both models answer.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig4_abstention.png}
\caption{Share of yes/no questions on which the model declines to answer when the image is removed ($m<0.5$;
95\% CIs by image). Top: the main run's instruction (``Answer with only yes or no''). Bottom: probe R2, whose
instruction allows ``unknown''.}
\label{fig:abst}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Agreement between prior and image.} Refusal is not the whole story: on the 436 questions where both
MedGemma-4B and Gemma-3 answer without the image ($m\ge0.9$), P3 is still +8.0\ci{2.9}{13.3}, and in the Qwen pair,
where nobody refuses, image removal still separates the models. A model whose blind guess matches what the image
shows gives the same answer with and without it, and image removal scores that as blind. MedGemma's blind answers
beat the majority-answer prior on PathVQA (P1a, +5.0; +11.9\ci{7.1}{16.6} among questions it answers, on data it
was not trained on), and its no-image answers agree with its image answers beyond chance ($\kappa=0.21$ \vs 0.11
for Gemma-3); in the Qwen pair it is the base whose blind answers agree more ($\kappa=0.16$ \vs 0.09), and the
base that image removal calls less reliant. The correctness split shows what MedGemma's excess consists of
(\cref{fig:p3}, bottom): \dang{}-and-correct is 39.2\% \vs 25.1\% (+14.1\ci{11.1}{17.1}), while
\dang{}-and-wrong, the cell that would mislead a user, is 11.3\% \vs 11.7\% ($-0.4$\ci{$-2.7$}{2.0});
MedGemma-1.5's excess is also correct (+9.3 correct, +0.5 wrong).

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_p3.png}
\caption{The MedGemma-4B $-$ Gemma-3 difference in \dang{} share under each probe and subset, and split by
whether the \dang{} answer is correct (paired; 95\% CIs by image).}
\label{fig:p3}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Outside the training data (probe R4)}
\label{sec:r4}
SLAKE is training data of both MedGemma releases (their evaluated images are disjoint from SLAKE's train split, but
the distribution and question templates are not) and not of MedVLThinker, so ``trained on SLAKE'' explains the
SLAKE results as well as ``uses the image more'' does. R4 repeats the opposite-answer probe on PathVQA, which
MedGemma's training explicitly excluded, for all five models (\cref{tab:tests}). Every model follows the partner
image on 43--49\% of the 1,192 swaps and is right on both images on 36--43\%, far from the 0\% of a model that
ignores the image: all five read pathology images, to a similar degree. MedGemma-4B does not differ from Gemma-3
(H12a: +0.8\ci{$-2.7$}{4.2}), MedGemma-1.5 follows \emph{less} (H12b: $-5.6$\ci{$-9.1$}{$-2.0$},
$p_{\text{Holm}}=0.003$), and MedVLThinker matches its base as predicted (H12c). Resampling PathVQA's 154 question
templates instead of images gives the same conclusions. Under the decision rule fixed before the run, the SLAKE gap
is reported as possibly a training-distribution effect, and the claim that either MedGemma uses the image more
than Gemma-3 is withdrawn. This matches accuracy: MedGemma's lead over Gemma-3 is 18 points on SLAKE yes/no and
2 on PathVQA (\cref{tab:acc}). On PathVQA the wrong-image and opposite-answer probes find no MedGemma-4B advantage;
only the black image does (+19.2), consistent with its reading an empty image as ``no findings'' rather than with
greater use of image content.

\subsection{The chance floor}
\label{sec:chance}
An answer counts as image-independent whenever the no-image answer equals the with-image answer, which on yes/no
questions happens often by chance. On the P3 set MedGemma's answers are unchanged without the image 58.6\% of the
time against 49.1\% expected from its answer distributions alone (Gemma-3: 49.7\% \vs 45.7\%). Combined with
consistency this gives a \textbf{chance floor of 41.5\% (MedGemma) and 35.8\% (Gemma-3)}, against observed
\dang{} shares of 50.5\% and 36.8\%. About 6 of the 13.7 points of P3 are the difference in floors, partly because
MedGemma is more consistent (84.5\% \vs 78.4\%), a desirable property the metric counts against it. Corrected for
chance, $\Delta\kappa=+0.112$\ci{0.044}{0.180}.

\subsection{Does image reliance flag wrong answers?}
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_selective.png}
\caption{AUROC for ranking correct above incorrect yes/no answers (test, 95\% CIs): the model's confidence
\vs label-free image reliance under each probe.}
\label{fig:sel}
\end{figure}

If image-independent answers were the unreliable ones, image reliance could serve as a warning signal. Ranking
each yes/no answer by its image PMI separates correct from incorrect answers at chance (\cref{fig:sel}; AUROC
\textbf{0.513}\ci{0.473}{0.552} for MedGemma, 0.532 for Gemma-3), while the model's own confidence reaches 0.709
and 0.603 (P2: better by 0.197\ci{0.145}{0.250} and 0.071\ci{0.026}{0.116}). Whether a model leaned on the image
does not tell us whether it was right.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{What image removal measures.} Removing the image asks a model a question about an image that is not
there. Its answer depends first on whether it will answer at all and on how good its priors are. Across three
pairs and three datasets, every difference image removal reported between a medical model and its base went
unconfirmed by the probes that keep an image in the input, and its largest differences coincided with the largest
differences in refusal. The original study's corroborating checks (black image, random swaps) agreed with image
removal on its chest X-ray models~\cite{sadanandan2026consistent}; on ours they do not. A \dang{} share is
therefore underspecified without its probe, and a comparison of \dang{} shares between models measured by image
removal can say more about refusal policy than about image use.

\paragraph{What the in-format probes measure.} The in-format probes are not neutral either. On SLAKE they say
both MedGemmas use the image far more than Gemma-3; on PathVQA, outside their training data, they say they do
not. A model's reliance on the image is a property of the model \emph{and} the data, and in-format probes run on a
model's training distribution can reflect what it learned there rather than how it uses images in general. For
these three pairs, no general claim that the medical model relies on the image more survives held-out data.

\paragraph{Where the residual risk is.} MedGemma's extra \dang{} answers are correct, and the stable,
image-independent and wrong cell is the same for both models. MedGemma's errors, fewer overall (25.7\% \vs
37.6\%), are more often of this kind (44\% \vs 31\%, +12.9\ci{6.0}{19.9}), so a consistency or reliance check
would miss them.

\paragraph{Recommendations for reliance audits.} (1)~Probe reliance in format, ideally with an image that calls
for a different answer, and report agreement between probes. (2)~Run in-format probes on data outside each
model's training set, and check training documentation before comparing models. (3)~Report the \dang{} share
with its chance floor or as $\kappa$; on balanced yes/no data a model whose blind answers are pure noise is about
50\% ``not reliant''. (4)~Split \dang{} by correctness. (5)~Allow abstention, and treat declining without an image
as desirable rather than as a format failure.

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
Three pairs from two model families show that image removal \emph{can} disagree with in-format probes and suggest
why; they do not estimate how often across the field. The refusal and prior-agreement accounts and the
per-dataset breakdown (\cref{fig:bydataset}) were formed after the primary results; of the dataset-specific
comparisons only R4 was registered. R4 covers one modality, pathology, on which all models are weak (pair accuracy
36--43\%), so it argues against a general advantage but cannot rule one out in every domain. R3 and the SLAKE
results rest on templated questions that recur across images; resampling templates instead of images leaves the
conclusions unchanged. MedGemma-4B was also trained on VQA-RAD, whose test images almost all occur in its train
split, so its VQA-RAD results may reflect exposure; the general models' training data are not published. Checkpoints
differ in their whole post-training, not only in medical data. Refusal is inferred from first-token mass and
confirmed on a sample by free generation. Paraphrase equivalence was judged by an LLM and \textbf{was not validated by
independent human raters}; a second check of 50 used paraphrases, rated by the author with AI assistance,
accepted 88\% (above the pre-specified 85\%), but it is not independent of AI judgment. This is the main
limitation of the consistency measure; the probe comparison does not use paraphrases. PathVQA questions are auto-generated and
often ungrammatical. The chance correction, correctness split and refusal split were added after seeing the
results. Excluding the 330 pilot questions used to tune the design leaves every conclusion unchanged (P1a
+6.3\ci{2.4}{10.6}, P3 +12.9\ci{8.9}{17.1}). Benchmark VQA is not clinical use, and nothing here is a clinical
claim.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
Is a small medical VLM consistent but blind? By the image-removal test MedGemma looks that way, more than its
general-purpose twin. No probe that keeps an image in the input agrees, in any dataset or pair we tested: image
removal measures whether a model answers without an image and whether its priors match the image. Probes that keep
the image find the medical models more image-reliant only on data they were trained on. Comparing models on image
reliance needs in-format probes on held-out data, chance correction and a correctness split.

\appendix
\section{Implementation details}
\label{sec:impl}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} A Python package (\texttt{medvlm}) with a command-line interface: \texttt{prepare}
(download, deterministic sampling, SHA-checked images), \texttt{paraphrase} (generation plus rule and judgment
validation, fail-closed), \texttt{pipeline} (resumable inference in parts with checkpoint analysis),
\texttt{probes} (R1--R3), \texttt{contrast} (R4), \texttt{analyze}, \texttt{compare}, \texttt{posthoc},
\texttt{replication} and \texttt{contamination} (all tables and figures here). Configs layer base, profile, model
and hardware settings. Each job is one (question, condition) pair keyed by ID, so interrupted runs resume without
recomputation, and every run records its config, commit and library versions. Registrations are git tags.

\paragraph{Inference.} PyTorch 2.11 and Hugging Face Transformers 5.19, bf16, SDPA attention, one RTX 4080 SUPER
(16\,GB). MedGemma-4B runs at 0.23\,s per call (18,896 calls in about 75 minutes, 8.2\,GB peak). During pre-flight
we found that in bf16 the \emph{batch size} changes teacher-forced log-probabilities by up to 1.09 nats (median
0.17) even with identical, unpadded inputs, while $P(\text{yes})$ changes by at most 0.008. An fp32 output head did
not remove it, so the cause is inside the network. All runs therefore use batch size 1, which costs about
1.5$\times$ throughput. A regression check reproduced the T4 pilot on the new GPU (98.5\% identical answers, mean
$|\Delta P(\text{yes})|=0.004$).

\paragraph{Testing.} 103 unit tests and 7 real-model tests cover, among others, scoring edge cases, paraphrase
rules (including each failure class found in the audit), batching equivalence, crash-safe resume, the coverage
of the clustered bootstrap (by simulation), the test-split restriction of P3, chance agreement of $\kappa$, the
construction of opposite-answer partners and an oracle-\vs-blind check of pair accuracy.

\section{Paraphrase equivalence rubric}
\label{app:rubric}
A pair is \textbf{accepted} only if it asks exactly the same thing, so the correct answer cannot differ.
Allowed: perception framing (``can X be seen'', ``is X visible'', ``can X be seen to be enlarged''), exact
synonyms (clavicle/collarbone, encephalon/brain, intravenous contrast/dye), reordering. \textbf{Rejected}: a
fact turned into a possibility or capability (``Is the heart enlarged?''$\to$``Can the heart be enlarged?'');
a broadened or narrowed term (mass$\to$lesion, organs$\to$structures, digestive system$\to$GI tract, skull
fracture$\to$cranial injury); a changed scope or presupposition (``Do the organs exist in X''$\to$``Are there
organs in X''); added qualifiers, findings or modality (``bilaterally'', ``on imaging studies'',
``radiograph''); a reversed or changed relation (``does A show B''$\to$``is A associated with B'', ``mass
lateral to X''$\to$``X lateral to mass''); antonyms (healthy$\leftrightarrow$unhealthy,
coronal$\to$transverse); two questions in one; malformed text. Rejections by class: relation 447, term 364,
modal 106, added content 102, organ$\to$structure 47, generic collapse 30, polarity 19, scope 9 (plus
template-pass rejections).
